boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Killdeer Mountain record (July 28-29, 1864) in Sully's Expedition Against the Sioux in Dakota Territory [July 1864]. The establishment of Fort Rice, the emigrant train and the August 8-9 fighting in the Little Missouri badlands are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives detachments from eight units (2,200) and the Santee and Teton Sioux without figures (US bounds 2,200 and 2,200); the live field reads 0. Sully lists his two brigades and says the whole force on the field numbered about 2,200; he puts the Indians at over 1,600 lodges and at least 5,000 or 6,000 warriors of the Unkpapas, Sans Arcs, Blackfeet, Minneconjous, Yanktonais and Santee. Thomas also gives 1,600 lodges. NPS gives Pope's planned force of about 2,500.
claims.rationale: Sully's July 28 field figure and his estimate of the opposing camp that day; NPS's 2,500 is the planned force, not a field count; the Indian figure is an opponent's estimate. No account by the Dakota bands was inspected; their numbers, aims and losses come from their opponents' estimates, prisoners' or scouts' statements relayed by them, or the NPS summary. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

NPS says Sully met some chiefs before attacking; the inspected July 31 report does not mention such a meeting, but says that the day after the fight Indians planted a white flag, were fired on by some men, and that he saw the flag too late.

claims.value: The frozen US commander is Brigadier General Alfred Sully. The frozen and live Native American commander is Inkpaduta (no rank; the live page tags him [CS], not adopted); none of the inspected reports names him, so his role is not established here. Sully directed Brackett to charge a large body on the right; Brackett says he asked and received permission to charge with sabers. Thomas commanded the Second Brigade on the left, and McLaren destroyed the camp on the 29th.
claims.rationale: Command roles from interested reports; no automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads Unknown; the live field reads 46 (US 15; CS 31). Sully judges the Indian killed at 100 to 150; Brackett's battalion found 27 dead in its sector (13 after the charge). The compiler's note on Sully's omitted list shows 2 killed and 8 wounded in Brackett's battalion, 1 killed and 1 wounded in the Sixth Iowa, 2 killed in the Second Minnesota Cavalry and 1 wounded in the Dakota cavalry; Thomas mentions two pickets killed on the 29th.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Brackett's 27 may be within Sully's estimate; the live 15 and 31 are not traced.

open_questions: Pope's report (read in its opening), Pollock's, Pattee's, Miner's, Stufft's, Pope's battery, Rogers's, Camp's, McLaren's and Adams's reports, the list of property destroyed (p.172), the Dakota bands' account and maps remain deferred. Brackett's report is the targeted follow-up for the casualty figures.

NPS/CWSAC (the live battle page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Sully's July 31, 1864 report and Thomas's August 1 report (Second Brigade) are interested accounts; Brackett's August 1 report is a separate family used as the follow-up. Sully also wrote the Whitestone Hill report in the 1863 pass. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.

No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting. Participants are named as the sources name them; characterizations in the sources (including 'hostile', 'savages', 'massacre' or 'battle') are quoted as the sources' own words and not adopted.
